newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa wonders where past will lead it.
newsitem.headline: South Africa wonders where past will lead it.

text.p: After a week of damaging claims by a state assassin, South Africans are finding that putting their troubled past behind them may be harder than they hoped.

Eugene de Kock, a convicted killer who was in the pay of the apartheid regime, is seeking to lighten his punishment by telling all in court about the men who gave him orders to liquidate black opponents of white rule.

A police colonel who ran a death squad, he implicated South Africa's last white presidents, F.W. de Klerk and P.W. Botha, and numerous smaller fish he says knew of the dirty-tricks campaign and even ordered civilian attacks.
"Like a spider at the centre of his web, de Kock has strings of intrigue reaching into the most secret, most villainous corners of apartheid's dark past," the Saturday Star newspaper said.
Botha is unrepentant, old and retired but de Klerk leads a reformed National Party which has disowned its apartheid past and aims to regain power by 2004.
He said de Kock's claims were nothing new. He has said sorry for, but distanced himself from, apartheid's excesses yet the past looks set to pursue him far into the future.
"It will take years to unravel truth from fiction in de Kock's long and bitter testimony," the Citizen daily said.
"In the interim, those whom he has named may find that the mud he has thrown will stick."

Anti-apartheid veterans feel vindicated in saying de Klerk is not as clean as he professes, but no-one really knows what to do with de Kock's "information" that, coming between conviction and sentencing, could not be challenged.
De Kock also alleged that close allies of President Nelson Mandela's main black rival, Mangosuthu Buthelezi, were in cahoots with the apartheid regime.
Mandela's ruling African National Congress called his testimony "the tip of the iceberg in the search for the truth".
South Africa is split. Some people demand retribution, some plead for reconciliation and the majority want both but don't know where to find the balance.
The divide has even been institutionalised, pitting the courts against the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which hopes to heal the past, with no clear battlelines.

State prosecutors are rushing ahead to try and build watertight cases against others suspected of apartheid-era crimes, while Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth commission is offering them amnesty if they tell and repent.
The situation is only simple for suspects who insist they are innocent and therefore cannot ask for amnesty.
The most prominent figure to do this is apartheid defence minister Magnus Malan, on trial with 15 others for a massacre allegedly committed by a state-backed hit squad.
But even plain retribution has its problems. Evidence is scarce and the defence has said, as the Malan trial nears its end, that the state has influenced witnesses.

In the most controversial tug-of-war between the courts and the commission, prosecutors have set a December trial date for Dirk Coetzee, who ran the secret death-squad before de Kock, then fled abroad to tell the world about it.
Tutu's commission says it will try to beat the courts by speeding up Coetzee's application for amnesty.
De Kock, who tried to kill Coetzee to silence him, is also applying for amnesty after belatedly confessing.
Some hope his testimony to the truth commission will provide harder evidence against those he has implicated, others that he will be proved to have lied.
Tutu hopes more perpetrators of human-rights abuses will testify -- from both sides of the struggle -- but many have got cold feet after seeing Coetzee face trial.

Tutu's commission, due to wind up in 1998, has been attacked from all sides, including families of murdered activists such as black consciousness leader Steve Biko who say killers should not get off just for saying sorry.
